summary_html: **Mandatory reporters** (designated professionals) must report suspected child abuse or neglect. Federal law sets the funding and policy floor (CAPTA) and mandates reporter frameworks on federal lands/facilities (VICAA).
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — federal floor for state reporting systems  
- **Victims of Child Abuse Act (34 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20307)** — includes federal-facility reporter duties (recodified from former 42 U.S.C. §13031)

primary_citations.citation_text: New York - N.Y. Soc. Serv. Law § 411 et seq. (Child Protective Services Act – reporting requirements)
New York - Family Court Act Article 10 (Abuse/Neglect juvenile proceedings)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Matter of Catherine G. v. County of Essex
key_cases.holding: The Court held that a fourteen-year-old sibling is not a 'person legally responsible' under Family Court Act § 1012, so mandated reporters had no statutory duty to report his abuse of his sisters and the mother's late notice of claim against county and school officials was patently meritless.
key_cases.relevance: This decision fixes the outer boundary of the mandated-reporter duty by defining who can be the subject of a reportable allegation.
key_cases.quote: When in doubt about whether a case must be reported under Social Services Law § 413, they ought to err on the side of caution and make a report

key_cases.case_name: Kimberly S.M. v. Bradford Central School
key_cases.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York, Fourth Department
key_cases.holding: The Fourth Department reversed summary judgment and reinstated the complaint, holding that a mandated reporter's duty under Social Services Law § 413 is measured by the facts known when abuse is suspected and that liability under § 420(2) is not defeated merely because the alleged abuser later proves not to have been a person legally responsible for the child.
key_cases.relevance: This is the principal New York decision imposing civil liability on a mandated reporter for a willful failure to report.
key_cases.quote: a mandated reporter is obligated to report suspected cases of child sexual abuse based upon facts and circumstances within the knowledge of the reporter

key_cases.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York, Third Department
key_cases.holding: The Third Department modified to dismiss the failure-to-report claims, holding that because a school employee who abused students was not a 'person legally responsible' for their care, the children were not 'abused children' for Social Services Law § 413 purposes and the school district could not be liable under § 420(2).
key_cases.relevance: It states the § 413 duty and the § 420(2) liability standard while confining both to abuse by a parent or person legally responsible.
key_cases.quote: Civil liability may be imposed upon these individuals who knowingly and willfully fail to make the requisite report

key_cases.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York, Second Department
key_cases.holding: The Second Department held that Social Services Law § 419 immunity required dismissal of the complaint against the hospital that reported suspected child abuse, since a person or institution participating in good faith in making a report is immune from civil and criminal liability and good faith is presumed for mandated reporters.
key_cases.relevance: Section 419 immunity and its presumption of good faith are the protection that makes the mandatory reporting duty workable.
key_cases.quote: We find, contrary to Special Term, that, by virtue of Social Services Law § 419, the foregoing complaint must be dismissed insofar as it is asserted against the defendant hospital
